rv.q: East Is East is an important piece of work for people such as myself, Arshad and much of the cast playing Khan’s children. The language of the play describes us as “half-caste”; I tend to use mixed-race and some of the cast prefer dual heritage. Whatever the preferred term, the play captures the nuance of growing up between cultures.
He raises his family in the Pakistani tradition but is blind to the impact upon them of cultural and generational changes which have arisen since he immigrated to the UK in 1930.

Bolton Octagon’s latest production is an anniversary revival of Ayub Khan Din’s East is East, a story that explores the complications of family, cultural identity and religion. George Khan has lived in England for 30 years and works hard to keep his Pakistani traditions alive whilst his seven children develop their own identities in 1970s Salford.
